questions.stem: How does branching affect a molecule's boiling point?

options.text: It lowers the boiling point by shrinking surface area
options.explanation: Fewer contact points weaken the induced attractions between branched molecules.

options.text: It raises the boiling point by adding bonds
options.explanation: Bond count inside the molecule does not set the boiling point.

options.text: It leaves the boiling point unchanged
options.explanation: Isomers with different shapes boil at different temperatures.

options.text: It removes electrons from the molecule
options.explanation: Branching rearranges the same atoms, keeping the electron count.

questions.stem: Why do heavier noble gases boil higher than lighter ones?

options.explanation: Thermal expansion is a consequence, not a cause.

options.text: More electrons give stronger and more frequent temporary dipoles
options.explanation: Growing electron clouds raise the induced attraction down the group.

options.text: Their nuclei carry positive charge that attracts neighbours
options.explanation: Nuclear charge stays internal; the interatomic pull is induced-dipole based.

options.text: They hydrogen bond in the liquid
options.explanation: Noble gases carry no hydrogen at all.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between molecular surface area and induced dipole strength?

options.text: Area has no bearing on the forces
options.explanation: The contact-points diagram exists precisely because it does.
Rearranging the same atoms preserves the count.

options.text: Larger area means more contact and stronger induced forces
options.explanation: Contact area is the multiplier on the London interaction.
More contact strengthens, not weakens, the attraction.

questions.stem: Two isomers share a formula and electron count but boil 25 degrees apart. What explains the gap?

options.text: The straighter isomer has more electrons
options.explanation: Identical formulas fix identical electron counts.
No O-H, N-H or H-F group appears in either.
Systematic isomer gaps are real chemistry.

options.text: The straighter isomer contacts neighbours over more area
options.explanation: At equal electrons, surface area decides the induced contribution.

questions.stem: Which pair of changes both raise a hydrocarbon's boiling point?

options.explanation: Both grow surface contact and electron count effects.
Branching cancels the chain-length gain by shrinking contact.
The shorter chain cuts electron count and lowers the point.
Both changes push the boiling point down.

questions.stem: State the effect of branching on boiling temperature and name the force involved.
questions.modelAnswer: Branching lowers the boiling temperature because it reduces the surface area over which London dispersion forces can act.

questions.stem: State what happens to temporary dipoles as electron count increases.
questions.modelAnswer: A greater electron count makes distortions more likely and bigger, so temporary dipoles are larger and more frequent and the induced forces strengthen.

questions.stem: Explain why the alkane boiling-point graph climbs with chain length.
questions.modelAnswer: Each extra carbon brings more electrons and more molecular surface, so both the size and the contact area of induced interactions grow, and the boiling point rises with every added CH2 unit.

questions.stem: Pentane boils at 36 degrees while its branched isomer 2-methylbutane boils at 28 degrees. How much branching credit, in degrees, does the straight chain claim in this pair?
questions.modelAnswer: The 8-degree gap is the branching premium: the straight chain's larger contact area holds it liquid to a higher temperature.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force dominates between alcohol molecules?

options.explanation: No metal atoms participate.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding through the O-H groups
options.explanation: Polarised hydrogens reach lone pairs on neighbouring oxygens.
That is the alkane's ceiling, not the alcohol's.
Alcohols are covalent molecular liquids.

questions.stem: Why is the hydrogen of an O-H group delta-positive?

options.explanation: Repulsion is not the polarity mechanism.
Carbon is not part of the O-H bond.

options.text: Oxygen draws the shared electron pair toward itself
options.explanation: High electronegativity leaves hydrogen's positive end exposed.
The pair is shared, not surrendered.

questions.stem: Propane boils at -42 degrees and propanol at 97 degrees. What is the dominant reason for the 139-degree gap?

options.explanation: The electron difference is minor; the force type does the heavy lifting.
Covalent strength does not set boiling points.
It is a covalent molecule.

options.text: Propanol's molecules hydrogen bond while propane's only induce dipoles
options.explanation: The force upgrade is the whole story.

questions.stem: Which statement about alkane intermolecular forces is correct?

options.text: Their only intermolecular forces are induced dipole-dipole
options.explanation: No permanent dipoles or O-H groups exist in a pure alkane.
C-H bonds are never hydrogen-bond donors.
The hydrocarbon skeleton is non-polar.

options.text: Their molecules attract by ion-induced dipole
options.explanation: No ions are present.

questions.stem: What structural feature must a molecule carry to hydrogen bond?

options.explanation: Neutral alcohols hydrogen bond readily.

options.text: Hydrogen attached to O, N or F
options.explanation: That kit is the donor requirement.
C-H hydrogens never qualify.
Unsaturation plays no role in hydrogen bonding.

questions.stem: Name the force that sets alcohol boiling points above alkane boiling points.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules sets their boiling points far above the induced dipole-dipole ceiling of alkanes.

questions.stem: Quote the boiling points of propane and propanol.
questions.modelAnswer: Propane boils at -42 degrees and propanol at 97 degrees, a 139-degree demonstration of the hydrogen-bond premium.

questions.stem: Explain why replacing a hydrogen of an alkane by an OH group changes the intermolecular force inventory.
questions.modelAnswer: The OH group adds a polar O-H bond whose hydrogen reaches oxygen lone pairs on neighbours, so hydrogen bonding joins the inventory; the pure alkane carried only induced dipole-dipole forces.

questions.stem: If ethanol boils at 78 degrees and its same-electron-count alkane analogue boils at -24 degrees, how many degrees of hydrogen-bond premium does ethanol show?
questions.modelAnswer: Subtracting -24 from 78 gives 102 degrees, the hydrogen-bond premium this comparison displays.

questions.stem: Which hydrogen halide boils highest?

options.explanation: HBr is an intermediate on the line.
HI tops the induced-only trend but not HF.
Hydrogen bonding lifts HF far above every neighbour on the series.
HCl sits at the trend line's low end.

questions.stem: Why do the boiling points of HCl, HBr and HI increase in order?

options.explanation: None of the three hydrogen bonds at all.
Bonds lengthen down the group.
Polarity actually falls as the halogen gets bigger.

options.text: Each molecule carries more electrons, strengthening induced forces
options.explanation: Electron count climbs down the group and so does the dispersion pull.

questions.stem: What two features of fluorine make strong hydrogen bonds possible in HF?

options.text: High bond polarity and small intense lone pairs
options.explanation: The polar bond exposes hydrogen; the compact lone pairs accept the link.
Fluorine is small and strongly electronegative.

options.text: Low electron count and high mass
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant; the count is nine.
Fluorine has neither.

questions.stem: HCl is a polar molecule yet sits on the trend line. Why does polarity alone not lift it?

options.explanation: Permanent dipoles do raise points above the induced baseline.

options.text: Its polarity supports only permanent dipole-dipole forces, which beat induced ones modestly at equal size
options.explanation: Without hydrogen bonding there is no premium.

options.text: HCl's polarity is too weak to matter at all
options.explanation: The polarity does contribute; it just cannot add the hydrogen-bond premium.

options.text: HCl carries hydrogen bonds like HF
options.explanation: Chlorine's diffuse lone pairs cannot form them.

questions.stem: Which statement about the hydrogen halide graph is correct?

options.explanation: HF boils highest of all four.
HI boils highest of the induced-only trio.

options.text: HCl, HBr and HI rise steadily while HF plots far above the extrapolated line
options.explanation: The smooth climb plus the outlier is exactly the data shape.

options.text: All four sit on one straight line
options.explanation: HF's outlier breaks the line.

questions.stem: State the force responsible for the smooth HCl-to-HI climb and the force responsible for HF's outlier position.
questions.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole forces drive the smooth climb, and hydrogen bonding accounts for HF's outlier position.

questions.stem: Describe what the fluorine end of an HF molecule offers to a neighbour.
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine offers small, intense lone pairs that accept the hydrogen bond from a neighbouring molecule's polarised hydrogen.

questions.stem: Explain why HF's boiling point exceeds HI's despite HI's far greater electron count.
questions.modelAnswer: HI's electron advantage strengthens only induced forces, whereas HF gains a whole extra force channel - hydrogen bonding - whose energy outweighs the electron-count deficit and hoists HF above the whole series.

questions.stem: If HF's hydrogen-bond premium adds roughly 180 degrees above its trend-line slot of about -80 degrees, estimate HF's actual boiling point.
questions.modelAnswer: Adding the premium to the slot gives about 100 degrees, close to HF's observed boiling point near 20 degrees once the trend slope is folded in.
